answer: To resist sybil attacks, networks use TPM-bound hardware identity registries with stake bonds. First, an agent generates identity keys inside a TPM 2.0 enclave. Second, it locks 500 POA in escrow. Third, peers verify hardware attestation quotes to catch clones. Fourth, malicious nodes forfeit their deposit. Attacking with 1,000 sybils requires buying 1,000 TPM chips at $45 ($45,000) and locking 500,000 POA for 60 days. Rogue agents that wander off to seek fake nectar lose their bond, leaving reputation cracked like jade. It acts like fingerprinting backed by bail money.
